What a rank shows

A belt or stripe marks progress a coach has seen. Sandy looks at a pattern of skill across mat tasks. A win, one move, or a class count alone falls short.

He looks for safe choices and skills that work. He also looks for how you adapt and choose. Read how we describe progress and how class tasks give us evidence.

What stripes mean

A stripe is a smaller step within a belt. Coaches may see different kinds of growth in two students. They can explain what changed for each person.

Safe training is the floor for practice. Tap early, release at once, and care for your partner. Those habits let you both learn.

A coach also looks for skills that work under pressure. Ask what they saw you do with more ease. Ask which task you can work on next.

What a belt means

A belt marks a broader stage of growth. Sandy weighs your range of skills and safe choices. He watches how you solve problems and adapt.

He also watches how much help you need. A belt makes that progress visible. The coach makes the rank decision.

Kids belt colors

The IBJJF youth system covers ages 4 to 15. Kids start with white. They can then move through these groups:

  • Grey-white, grey, and grey-black.
  • Yellow-white, yellow, and yellow-black.
  • Orange-white, orange, and orange-black.
  • Green-white, green, and green-black.

Each color group has age rules. As a child grows, adult ranks and their rules become relevant. Ask the coach which rule fits your child.

Adult belt order

The order is white, blue, purple, brown, then black. The IBJJF rank rules set age and time limits. We use them as a guide, with Sandy's judgment of readiness.

IBJJF age and time rules

The June 11, 2026 rules set these age floors. Blue and purple begin at 16. Brown begins at 18. Black can begin at 18 for a brown-belt Adult World Champion.

Other black-belt cases have their own age rules. Use the full IBJJF rules for those cases and exceptions.

Adult minimum time is two years at blue. It is one and a half years at purple. It is one year at brown. Check the rules for exceptions that fit an athlete's record.

The IBJJF counts these periods from rank registration. That means the date you register each belt with them. Time on its own is separate from coach readiness.

A black belt can request the first degree after three years of proven activity. Read the degree guide and the IBJJF source for the full terms.

Four kinds of skill evidence

1. Protect

You keep yourself and your partner safe as tasks get harder. You give useful resistance that lets both people learn. You tap early, release at once, and speak up.

2. Recognize and solve

You see the mat problem and find a useful answer. You can solve more kinds of problems with safe resistance. You show steady skill across key positions.

3. Adapt

You notice when the problem changes. You try another useful path when the first one fails. You keep both partners safe as you change.

4. Express

You choose useful paths with less coach help. Your choices fit your body, timing, and goals. You can explain what you are trying to do.

How the Report Card fits

The Report Card helps a coach record what they see. It keeps observations in one place. The coach still judges the whole pattern.

A card state, win count, or class count is separate from a rank decision. Class time gives you chances to practice and show skill. The coach uses that evidence to judge progress.

Care for the room

Train with care for your partner. Listen when the coach sets a safety rule. Use skill and a pace both partners can follow.

Practice the basics and respect each person's pace. These are shared class expectations. Rank also calls for growth in your grappling skill.

How parents can help

Ask your child what feels easier now. Ask what they are working on next. Let Sandy explain the change he has seen.

Celebrate that change at home. Keep daily enjoyment part of the goal. Focus on your child's path and their next useful task.

Common rank questions

How many stripes can a belt have?

Many schools use up to four stripes. Coaches use different systems. Ask Sandy how he uses them here.

How long does a rank take?

Each student's path is different. Sandy looks for a broad pattern of useful skill. He makes the call when the evidence supports it.

How can I see my child's progress?

Watch how they handle harder tasks. Look for safe choices and less need for prompts. Ask how they adapt when a move fails.

Read how often rank changes happen. Use the IBJJF source for rank rules.
